# Collaborative Code Editor — Production Architecture

## 0. Decisions at a glance

| Concern | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Conflict resolution | **YATA-style CRDT** (Yjs semantics), server-relayed | Offline-first, lease-based failover without history reconstruction, no transform-function bug class |
| Sync ordering | **Server-assigned monotonic `seq` per document**, not state vectors | Bus traffic and sync cost become O(gateways), not O(replicas). Eliminates 50k-entry state vectors |
| Fan-out | **Per-doc pub/sub topic + edge-local fan-out**, coalesced at 10 Hz | Bus traffic scales with edge nodes, not subscribers |
| Writer concurrency | **Hard cap 500 concurrent writers/doc**; overflow → observer tier | Physics, not policy — see §1.3 |
| Observers | **Viewport-scoped, coalesced 2 Hz**; >5k → HTTP diff polling | 95% of "50k on one doc" traffic is read-only |
| Presence | **Ephemeral awareness channel**, RoaringBitmap viewport index, shed first | Never in the CRDT, never persisted |
| Persistence | **Kafka as WAL + periodic zstd CRDT snapshots in S3** | Durable-before-ack is unnecessary; clients hold pending ops |
| Topology | **Home-region single-writer per doc, fenced lease** | Cross-region CRDT merge is possible but the log ordering isn't worth it |

---

## 1. Workload model and capacity math

### 1.1 The ambiguity that determines the architecture

"50,000 concurrent users editing the same documents" has two very different readings:

- **A:** 50k concurrent sessions platform-wide, Zipf-distributed across documents.
- **B:** 50k concurrent users inside *one* document.

These need different machinery. I design for A as the steady state and B as a supported degraded mode, because B is where the architecture either holds or falls over.

### 1.2 Assumed distribution (peak)

| Bucket | Documents | Concurrent editors/doc |
|---|---|---|
| Median | ~50,000 | 1–2 |
| p90 | ~2,000 | 4–10 |
| p99 | ~200 | 20–60 |
| Hot | ~20 | 100–500 |
| Pathological | 1–2 | 500 writers + 49,500 observers |

### 1.3 The physics constraint (why writers are capped)

Full op broadcast to `W` writers at `R` updates/sec costs `W²·R` messages/sec. At W = 50,000, R = 2: **5 × 10⁹ messages/sec**. No topology fixes this — it's not a sharding problem, it's arithmetic. Three escape hatches exist:

1. **Reduce R** — coalesce into ticks (10 Hz). Necessary but insufficient alone.
2. **Reduce W** — cap concurrent writers. Required.
3. **Reduce fan-out degree** — edge-local fan-out so the bus sees `gateways × ticks`, not `clients × ticks`. Required.

All three are in the design. With them, 50k *observers* + 500 *writers* on one document is comfortable:

```
Room server:  500 writers × 2 upd/s = 1,000 CRDT merges/s → 10 ticks/s
Bus:          64 gateways × 10 ticks/s = 640 msgs/s × 600 B = 384 KB/s   (trivial)
Per gateway:  800 local subscribers × 10 ticks/s = 8,000 msg/s = 4.8 MB/s
Observers:    2 Hz × 780 per gateway = 1,560 msg/s, viewport-filtered → ~200 msg/s actual
```

Note the key property: **bus load is independent of subscriber count.**

### 1.4 Global capacity targets

| Metric | Target |
|---|---|
| Concurrent sessions | 50,000 peak |
| Update ingress | 100k/s sustained, 300k/s 10s burst |
| Median update size | 120 B (p99 2 KB) |
| Ingress bandwidth | 12–25 MB/s |
| Egress bandwidth | 120–150 MB/s peak (dominant cost) |
| Local→remote edit latency | p50 45 ms, p99 150 ms (same region) |
| Document activation (cold) | p99 250 ms |

---

## 2. Conflict resolution

### 2.1 Data structures

```text
ID          := { replica: u64, clock: u32 }        // 12 B packed, varint 7–12 B

Item        := {
  id:          ID,
  originLeft:  ID | null,      // item immediately to the left at insert time
  originRight: ID | null,      // item immediately to the right at insert time
  content:     Run<utf8> | Tombstone | Embed,
  // Run is run-length merged: "function foo() {" is ONE item, not 16.
}

StructStore := Map<replica: u64, Item[]>           // dense array indexed by clock
DeleteSet   := Map<replica: u64, Interval[]>       // sorted, coalesced [start, end)

Snapshot    := { structs: StructStore, deletes: DeleteSet,
                 stateVector: Map<replica, u32>, seq: u64 }
Update      := { structs: Item[] /* new only */, deletes: DeleteSet,
                 replica: u64, clockLo: u32, clockHi: u32 }
```

**Merge rule (YATA):** items sharing the same `originLeft` are ordered by comparing their `originRight` positions, with `replica` ID as the deterministic tiebreak. The result is a total order that is **commutative, associative, and idempotent** — any permutation of updates converges to the same document. That property is what buys every failure-tolerance guarantee in §6.

**Run-length merging is load-bearing.** Without it, metadata is ~14 B/character; with it, a typed word is one item at ~14 B total. Typical code files land at **1.5–2.5× the raw text size in heap**, not 14×.

### 2.2 Replica IDs — do not use random 32-bit

At 50,000 random 32-bit IDs the birthday collision probability is `1 − exp(−n²/2N) ≈ 25%`. A collision silently corrupts the document (two writers claim the same clock). Use **server-assigned 64-bit IDs** from a per-document allocator (`(docEpoch << 32) | counter`), never client-generated.

### 2.3 Sync protocol — log-based, not state-vector-based

Because the room server assigns a total order, clients sync against the **log**, not against a state vector:

```text
C→S  Hello      { docId, lastSeq }            // 0 = first sync
S→C  Snapshot   { crdtBytes, seq }            // if lastSeq == 0 or gap > 5,000
S→C  Catchup    { updates[], seq }            // else: log range (lastSeq, head]
C→S  Update     { crdtBytes, clientSeq }      // local edits, optimistic
S→C  Ack        { clientSeq, seq }            // after durable append
S↔C  Aware      { bytes }                     // separate channel, unacked
S→C  Redirect   { roomNode }                  // on shard move
```

This is the single most important structural choice. A naive CRDT design ships a state vector to every client; for a document with 50k historical editors that's ~600 KB per sync message. Log-based sync makes steady-state sync **O(delta)**, and the server is the only party that ever holds a large state vector.

CRDT is still required — for offline merge, optimistic local apply, and lease failover — but it is no longer in the critical sync path.

### 2.4 Why CRDT over OT

| Dimension | OT + sequencer | YATA CRDT |
|---|---|---|
| Wire size per edit | 20–40 B | 60–150 B |
| Server memory | ~1.0× text | 15–2.5× text (+ tombstones, GC'd) |
| Offline editing | Requires rebase/undo machinery, frequently buggy | Native |
| Room failover | Rebuild transform history or block writes | Lease handoff, merge converges |
| Multi-writer servers | Impossible without a single sequencer | Any node can merge |
| Correctness risk | Transform functions have a long history of obscure n² bugs | Mature, fuzzed libraries |
 **Hot-doc sharding** | Blocked by sequencer | Possible but semantically useless for code |

**Verdict:** CRDT. The costs (2× memory, larger ops) are bounded for source files and mitigated by GC + run merging. OT would win if documents were >50 MB or a single doc needed >5,000 ops/s — neither applies to a code editor.

### 2.5 Code-specific conflict handling

CRDTs guarantee *textual* convergence, not *semantic* correctness. Two engineers editing the same function produce a valid merge that may not compile. Handle it honestly:

- **Atomic transactions.** Format-on-save, rename-symbol, and auto-import are multi-range edits. Wrap them in a single `Update` so peers never see a torn intermediate state.
- **Formatting vs. concurrent edits.** Advisory soft-lock on format, plus transform the format op against concurrent changes at the CRDT layer (3-way merge on item IDs). If the merge is ambiguous, refuse and re-run.
- **Post-merge diagnostics.** Run the parser/LSP on the merged state; surface a "concurrent edit" gutter marker where two authors touched overlapping ranges within the same window. Don't attempt semantic auto-repair.
- **LSP results are derived state.** Never merge them into the document CRDT. They are keyed by document version and cached per-version.
- **Binaries and large files** (>10 MB) exit CRDT mode entirely: file-level lock + git-style merge on commit.

---

## 3. Transport and fan-out topology

```
                    ┌──────────────┐
   clients ──WSS──▶ │ Edge Gateway │ ×64   (800 conns each, TLS, auth, rate limit)
                    └──────┬───────┘
                           │ subscribe: doc topics it has clients for
                    ┌──────▼───────┐
                    │  Pub/Sub Bus │  per-doc topics, interest-routed (NATS/Kafka)
                    └──────┬───────┘
                           │
                    ┌──────▼───────┐
                    │ Room Server  │ ×N   (virtual actor per doc, leased)
                    │  CRDT state  │
                    └──────┬───────┘
                           │
              ┌────────────┴────────────┐
              ▼                         ▼
        Kafka (WAL, 7d)          S3 (snapshots, zstd)
```

**Edge gateway.** Stateless except for the connection. Terminates TLS, validates the JWT, enforces per-connection rate limits (60 updates/s, 30 presence/s, 1 MB max frame), and maintains the local subscription set. A crash costs its 800 clients a reconnect, nothing more.

**Pub/sub bus.** One topic per document. Gateways subscribe to topics for documents their clients are in. Interest-based routing keeps subscription count proportional to *active docs × gateways with interest*, not to sessions. **The critical scaling property: bus message rate = gateways × ticks, independent of subscriber count.**

**Room server.** A virtual actor keyed by `docId` (Orleans/Akka model). Owns the authoritative CRDT state, assigns `seq`, coalesces, and publishes. Activates on first client, snapshots and deactivates after 10 min idle.

### 3.1 Coalescing is mandatory

The room server does not broadcast individual updates. It applies them to the CRDT immediately (for correctness and acking) and **emits a merged delta on a 100 ms tick** to writers and a 500 ms tick to observers.

A 100 ms tick at 1,000 updates/s collapses ~100 ops into one frame. Because run-length merging combines same-region edits, a coalesced frame is typically 400–800 B regardless of op count. This is a **20–100× reduction** in fan-out cost and is the difference between feasible and impossible.

### 3.2 Viewport-scoped subscription

Subscribers register a viewport (`[lineStart, lineEnd]`). The room server maintains:

```text
viewportIndex : Map<blockIdx: u32, RoaringBitmap<clientId>>
blockSize     : 100 lines
```

Cursor moves update two bitmaps. On each tick, an update touching block `b` fans out only to `viewportIndex[b]`. For a 10,000-line file with 50k observers spread across it, each update reaches ~1/100th of them. Roaring bitmaps make the union cheap (50k bits = 6 KB uncompressed, ~1 KB compressed).

### 3.3 Observer tier

Beyond 500 concurrent writers, clients join as observers:

- Read-only, 2 Hz coalesced deltas, viewport-filtered.
- Above **5,000 observers**, switch them off WebSocket to **HTTP diff polling**: `GET /doc/{id}/diff?since={seq}&viewport={a}-{b}`, served from an edge cache keyed on `(seq, viewport)`. Many observers share viewports, so hit rates are high and egress collapses onto the CDN.
- Observers see a "request edit access" affordance; a slot frees when a writer goes idle 60 s.

**Rejected alternative: region-sharding the document.** Splitting a file into independently-mergeable regions would allow 50k writers, but a code file is not partitionable that way (imports, types, and braces cross regions), and 1,000 simultaneous cursors is already unreadable. The product cap is correct.

---

## 4. Presence

Presence is high-frequency, low-value, and loss-tolerant. It gets its own channel, its own throttles, and the lowest priority under load.

```text
Awareness   := Map<replica: u64, Entry>
Entry       := {
  clock:    u32,               // per-replica monotonic, LWW tiebreak
  ttl:      u32,               // 30 s, refreshed by heartbeat
  user:     u64,
  cursor:   { anchor: RelPos, head: RelPos },
  viewport: [lineStart, lineEnd],
  mode:     Editing | Reading | Idle,
}
RelPos      := { replica: u64, clock: u32, offset: u16 }   // CRDT-relative, survives edits
```

**Cursor positions must be CRDT-relative.** An absolute character index is invalid the moment anyone upstream inserts text. Store the `ID` of the item the cursor follows plus an in-run offset, and resolve to an index at render time.

**Protocol.** Per-replica monotonic clock, last-writer-wins per replica, 30 s TTL with 10 s heartbeat. Expired entries are swept lazily. Presence is **never persisted** and **never merged into the document CRDT** — doing so would create tombstones for cursor movement and bloat the document permanently.

**Rate control.** Clients throttled to 20 Hz; server broadcasts at 5 Hz; entries coalesced to the latest state only.

**Scale handling.** Above ~200 peers in a viewport, showing individual cursors is useless. The room server switches to:
- **Top-50 nearest peers** by viewport distance, individually rendered.
- **Aggregate heatmap** from the bitmap: `popcount(viewportIndex[b])` per block, published at 1 Hz. Cheap, and it's what users actually want ("40 people are reading this section").

**Load shedding priority** (enforced at the edge and the room server):
1. Shed presence first — it degrades gracefully and rebuilds in <2 s from heartbeats.
2. Shed observer deltas — observers tolerate 5 s staleness.
3. Shed writer deltas — writers fall back to 2 Hz coalesced.
4. **Never shed acks.**

---

## 5. Persistence

### 5.1 Model

```
Document(docId, t) = Snapshot(seq = S) ⊕ Log(S+1 .. t)
```

```text
LogEntry  := { docId, seq: u64, replica: u64, clockLo: u32, clockHi: u32,
               update: bytes, ts: i64, epoch: u32 }        // epoch = fencing token
Manifest  := { docId, snapshotKey, snapshotSeq, lastSeq, sizeBytes, updatedAt }
```

### 5.2 Write path — broadcast first, append async

The obvious design is append-then-broadcast, costing ~5 ms of latency per edit. **It isn't necessary**, because clients retain pending ops until acked:

1. `t=0` — apply update to in-memory CRDT, publish to the bus.
2. `t=0` — enqueue to Kafka (`acks=all`, `linger.ms=2`), and to a local WAL for crash recovery.
3. `t≈5ms` — on broker ack, send `Ack{clientSeq, seq}`.

If the room server dies before the Kafka append, unacked clients re-send on reconnect. Clients that did receive the broadcast merge normally. **The CRDT's idempotence plus per-client pending queues make the log append effectively at-least-once with no data loss and no added latency.** This is the single best trade available here.

Idempotent apply key: `(replica, clockLo)`. Duplicate log entries are harmless.

### 5.3 Snapshots

- **Trigger:** every 5,000 updates, 60 s, or 8 MB of log tail — whichever first.
- **Content:** encoded `StructStore` + `DeleteSet` + state vector + `seq`, zstd-compressed.
- **Location:** S3, immutable, keyed `snapshots/{docId}/{seq}.zst`; manifest in Postgres.
- **Cadence:** ~2,000 active docs → ~33 snapshot writes/s. Negligible.
- **Retention:** latest + hourly for 24 h + daily for 90 d. This is the version-history mechanism — "undo to yesterday" is a replay from a checkpoint, not per-keystroke history.

### 5.4 Compaction and GC

- **Log compaction:** Kafka retention (7 days) plus explicit deletion below `min(snapshotSeq)` across replicas, keeping 24 h of overlap for point-in-time recovery.
- **Tombstone GC:** enable CRDT GC — deleted content collapses to bare `ID` tombstones. Trade-off: unbounded undo from document state is sacrificed. Undo becomes per-client (local ops only, via an UndoManager) and cross-user history comes from the snapshot chain. Correct call: the memory ceiling matters more than infinite undo.

### 5.5 Read path (cold document)

```
manifest lookup (Postgres, 2ms) → S3 GET snapshot (40ms) → zstd decode (10ms)
  → replay log tail from snapshotSeq+1 (5–30ms) → activate room actor
```

p99 ≈ 250 ms. Warm activation is a Redis-level pointer swap.

### 5.6 Storage math

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Log ingress | 100k × 120 B ≈ 12 MB/s → ~1 TB/day |
| Hot log (7 d) | ~7 TB |
| Snapshot working set | 2,000 docs × 200 KB × 2.5 ≈ 1 GB/generation |
| Retained (90 d daily + 24 h hourly) | ~200 GB |

---

## 6. Failure modes

| # | Failure | Detection | Behavior | RTO / RPO |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Client network partition | WS heartbeat miss (15 s) | Client buffers in IndexedDB (cap 50 MB / 24 h), applies optimistically. On reconnect sends `Hello{lastSeq}` → server returns log delta or snapshot; local unpushed ops merge via CRDT. | 0 / 0 |
| 2 | Gateway crash | LB health check (2 s) | 800 clients reconnect. **Jittered backoff** (full jitter, 100 ms base, 30 s cap) + token-bucket admission at 5k reconnects/s/region prevents a thundering herd. Resume from `lastSeq`. | <5 s / 0 |
| 3 | Room server crash | Lease heartbeat (2 s) | Lease expires in 5 s; new owner loads snapshot + replays log. Clients stall 2–5 s, then flush buffered ops. No loss (unacked clients re-send). | 5 s / 0 |
| 4 | Split brain (two room owners) | Fencing token mismatch at Kafka produce | Lease carries a monotonic `epoch`; the log rejects writes with a stale epoch. CRDT would converge anyway, but fencing prevents duplicate `seq` allocation. | <1 s / 0 |
| 5 | Kafka unavailable | Produce timeout (3 s) | Room server spills to local WAL (15 min / 500 MB buffer). Beyond that, **enters read-only mode and rejects writes** rather than dropping ops silently. | n/a / 0 |
| 6 | Hot-document storm | Subscriber count, per-doc update rate, per-connection queue depth | Circuit breaker: >500 writers → observer tier; >5,000 observers → HTTP polling; queue depth > 2 MB → downgrade that client to snapshot-only frames. | automatic |
| 7 | CRDT metadata blowup | Room heap, item count per doc | Run merging + GC + snapshot-and-restart of the actor (reload from snapshot to defragment heap). Hard cap at 20 MB text / 200k items → "large file mode" (locking, no CRDT). | <30 s |
| 8 | Malformed / poisoned update | Schema validation at edge, decoder fuzz suite | Reject frame, increment abuse counter, disconnect at threshold. Max 1 MB/frame, max 10k items/frame. | immediate |
| 9 | Presence storm | Per-client message rate | Throttle at 20 Hz, coalesce at server, shed presence entirely under load. | automatic |
| 10 | Region failure | Control-plane health | Promote the cross-region replica; it already has snapshots + async log (RPO ≈ 1 s). Clients re-push pending ops, so the effective RPO is 0 for anything the user saw. | 60 s / ~0 effective |
| 11 | Snapshot corruption | Periodic convergence check: hash doc state on two independent replays | Fall back to the previous snapshot generation + longer log replay. Snapshots are immutable and versioned, so this is always possible. | 30 s / 0 |
| 12 | Undo/redo across users | — | Per-client UndoManager tracking only local ops. A user cannot undo another user's edit; that is a product decision, not a limitation to engineer around. | n/a |

**Convergence verification.** A background job replays a random sample of documents from snapshot + log on an isolated process and compares a Merkle hash of the resulting CRDT state against the live room server. Divergence indicates a decoder or merge bug and pages immediately. CRDT bugs are silent; this is the only reliable detector.

---

## 7. Operational notes

**Observability per document:** subscriber count by tier, update rate, coalescing ratio, merge p99, log lag, snapshot age, heap. **Per-fleet:** reconnect rate, shed counters by priority, convergence-check failures. **Synthetic canaries:** bot editors typing on real documents 24/7, asserting round-trip convergence and latency SLOs.

**Security:** JWT with doc-scoped claims, 5 min TTL. ACL is checked at the gateway *and* re-verified at the room server every 60 s (defense in depth — a revoked user must not keep writing because a gateway cached a token). All frames size-capped and schema-validated; the CRDT decoder is fuzzed continuously.

**Cost envelope at 50k peak:** dominated by egress. ~120–150 MB/s peak, roughly 150 TB/month at 40% duty cycle → ~$8–15k/month egress; compute (64 gateways, ~40 room nodes, Kafka at 250k ops/s, S3) adds ~$25–40k. Viewport filtering and the observer polling path cut egress 3–5× versus naive broadcast. Total order: **$50–90k/month**, and the egress line is the one worth optimizing.

---

## 8. Trade-off summary

| Choice | Cost accepted | Benefit gained |
|---|---|---|
| CRDT over OT | 2× memory, 3× wire size | Offline, lease failover, no transform bugs |
| Log-based sync over state vectors | Server must track `seq`; no P2P | O(delta) sync instead of O(50k replicas) |
| 10 Hz coalescing | +100 ms perceived latency | 20–100× fan-out reduction — makes the system possible |
| Broadcast-before-append | Log is not the ack source of truth | −5 ms per keystroke, zero loss via client re-push |
| 500-writer cap | Product limitation | 50k-writer broadcast is arithmetically impossible |
| Viewport subscription | Cursors outside the viewport are stale | Fan-out proportional to visible content |
| Presence unpersisted | Lost on room failure, rebuilt in 2 s | No CRDT bloat, shed-first under load |
| Tombstone GC | No infinite undo from doc state | Bounded memory |
| Home-region single writer | Cross-region writes pay WAN RTT | Simple total order, fast, safe failover |

---

## 9. Phasing

1. **v1 — correct and single-region.** CRDT, log-based sync, coalesced fan-out, 500-writer cap, Kafka WAL + S3 snapshots. Ship the convergence verifier from day one; it is not optional for a CRDT system.
2. **v2 — the read path.** Observer tier, viewport bitmaps, HTTP diff polling above 5k observers. This is what makes hot documents survivable.
3. **v3 — multi-region.** Leased home-region writer, cross-region read replicas from snapshots, async log replication, region failover drills.

The design holds at 50k concurrent users, and at 50k users on a single document in the only mode that is physically achievable: a bounded set of writers plus an unbounded, cheap, viewport-filtered read path.

# Congestion control on a 400 ms / 200 Mbit/s path

## 1. The path's defining number: BDP

BDP = 200 Mbit/s × 0.400 s = **80 Mbit = 10 MB** (≈ 6,849 segments of 1,460 B).

Everything that goes wrong follows from this. The pipe holds 10 MB in flight at any instant, and the control loop has an **800 ms dead time** (400 ms forward + 400 ms back). A sender must have ~10 MB of unacknowledged data outstanding just to keep the link busy, and it learns about a full bottleneck 400 ms after the fact.

A 400 ms path without window scaling is hard-capped at 65,535 B / 0.4 s = **1.31 Mbit/s** (0.65% of capacity) — so WS ≥ 8 (16.8 MB) and timestamps are table stakes before any algorithm discussion.

## 2. Failure mode A — slow start is measured in seconds, not milliseconds

IW10 = 14,600 B is **0.146% of BDP**. Doubling per RTT: 14,600 × 2ⁿ = 10 MB requires n = log₂(685) ≈ **9.4 RTTs ≈ 3.8 s**.

During that ramp the link averages 10 MB / 3.8 s ≈ **21 Mbit/s — 10.6% utilization**, i.e. ~90% idle for four seconds. And slow start exits *on loss*, so it overshoots to BDP + buffer before backing off. A 1 MB RPC on this path finishes entirely inside slow start: 7 RTTs = 2.8 s for 1 MB ≈ **2.9 Mbit/s average**.

This is the dominant cost for web/RPC traffic and no amount of steady-state cleverness fixes it. HyStart++ (pacing-based exit) and larger IW help marginally; only a model-based sender or a split proxy really does.

## 3. Failure mode B — additive increase is a rounding error

Reno congestion avoidance adds 1 MSS per RTT = 1,460 B / 0.4 s = **29.2 kbit/s per RTT**, or **0.0146% of link capacity per RTT**.

To climb from zero to 200 Mbit/s in congestion avoidance takes 25 MB / 1,460 B = 17,123 RTTs = **1.9 hours**. After a single loss at W = 6,849 segments, halving to 3,424 and recovering takes 3,425 RTTs = **1,370 s ≈ 23 minutes**.

This only works if losses are rare. They are not.

## 4. Failure mode C — the required loss rate is unattainable

Mathis: BW ≤ (MSS/RTT) × 1.22/√p = 4,453/√p B/s on this path. Solving for 200 Mbit/s:

**p ≤ 3.2 × 10⁻⁸** — one loss per 31.5 million packets, i.e. per **46 GB**.

| Packet loss p | Reno throughput | % of 200 Mbit/s |
|---|---|---|
| 10⁻⁷ | 112.6 Mbit/s | 56% |
| 10⁻⁶ | 35.6 Mbit/s | 17.8% |
| 10⁻⁵ | 11.3 Mbit/s | 5.6% |
| 10⁻⁴ | 3.56 Mbit/s | 1.8% |
| 10⁻³ | 1.13 Mbit/s | 0.56% |
| 10⁻² | 0.36 Mbit/s | 0.18% |

Public Internet paths run 10⁻⁶–10⁻³. At 1% random loss this 200 Mbit/s path delivers **356 kbit/s**. The mechanism: at p = 10⁻⁵ a loss event arrives every 5.8 s of full-rate sending, while recovery takes 1,370 s. Losses arrive **236× faster than AIMD can repair them**, so cwnd pins at the Mathis fixed point and never grows.

Add recovery cost: fast retransmit costs 1 RTT (400 ms) per loss event; without SACK, k losses per window cost k RTTs. An RTO on this path is SRTT + 4·RTTVAR ≈ 440 ms and collapses cwnd to 1 MSS — a **3.8 s slow-start penalty** from one spurious timeout.

## 5. Bufferbloat — the loss-based equilibrium *is* a standing queue

Loss-based CC only stops growing when a packet is dropped, so equilibrium in-flight = BDP + B_buffer. The queue is not transient; it is the operating point.

| Buffer | Standing queue delay | RTT seen |
|---|---|---|
| 1 MB | 40 ms | 440 ms |
| 2.5 MB | 100 ms | 500 ms |
| 10 MB (1×BDP) | 400 ms | **800 ms** |
| 25 MB | 1,000 ms | 1.4 s |

The feedback loop makes it self-reinforcing: 10 MB of buffer → 800 ms RTT → BDP becomes 20 MB → the flow now needs 20 MB in flight → deeper buffer. Delay is quadratic in buffer size for a fixed rate.

The signature is a **sawtooth in delay**, not just in cwnd. With a 10 MB buffer, a single CUBIC flow oscillates between 400 ms (queue empty) and 800 ms (queue full), with a period of ~22 s (CUBIC's K at W_max = 13,698 segments is 17–22 s). That is a 400 ms peak-to-peak latency swing every twenty seconds — fatal for VoIP (<150 ms one-way) and interactive traffic, and invisible to throughput benchmarks.

Note this is *not* statistical queueing: M/M/1 at ρ=0.95 with 60 µs packet service time gives only ~1.1 ms of delay. Bufferbloat is entirely the standing queue that loss-based CC deliberately builds.

And the shallow-buffer trap: Appenzeller sizing says 10 MB/√N — with 100 flows, a 1 MB buffer (40 ms). But loss-based CC on this path *needs* the deep buffer to avoid the loss that would cut it in half. Shrink the buffer and you trade bloat for a 50% cwnd cut every few seconds.

## 6. CUBIC — the partial fix, and its residual failures

CUBIC replaces linear growth with W(t) = C(t−K)³ + W_max, C = 0.4, β = 0.7, in wall-clock seconds. Recovery time from a loss at W_max = 6,849 segments:

K = (0.3 × 6,849 / 0.4)^(1/3) = **17.3 s** vs Reno's 1,370 s — **79× faster**, and RTT-independent by construction.

But CUBIC still:
- **Requires loss to back off**, so the Mathis ceiling still applies (it's ~30% less loss-sensitive than Reno, not loss-immune). It still collapses to a few Mbit/s at 10⁻³.
- **Still bloats**: it fills to BDP + B just like Reno, and its convex region (dW/dt = 3C(t−K)²) is *more* aggressive per RTT on long paths — at t−K = 10 s, growth is 120 segments/s = 560 kbit/s per RTT, 19× Reno's rate. On a 400 ms path CUBIC out-competes Reno flows, and its residual RTT bias is ~RTT^−0.25 (vs Reno's RTT^−1): a 400 ms flow gets ~1.8× less than a 40 ms flow, not 10× less.
- **Crawls at small cwnd**: in the TCP-friendly region (W_cubic < W_est) it degenerates to Reno, which is exactly where short flows live — hence the 2.9 Mbit/s for a 1 MB transfer.

## 7. What actually fixes it

**R (v1/v2/v3)** — the structural change. It estimates BtlBw and RTprop from delivery-rate and RTT samples and paces at `pacing_gain × BtlBw` (1.25 / 0.75 / 1.0 in the 8-phase PROBE_BW cycle), with `cwnd = cwnd_gain × BDP` (gain 2.0 → 20 MB here). It does not treat random loss as congestion, so at p = 10⁻³ it still delivers ~180–200 Mbit/s where Reno gets 1.1. Its startup uses gain 2/ln2 = 2.885, so it still takes ~9–10 rounds ≈ 3.8 s to fill — the startup tax is unchanged; only the steady state and post-loss behaviour are fixed. BBRv1's costs: it holds ~1.25–1.5× BDP of queue (200 ms here), can starve CUBIC flows (~40% share in mixed deployments), and needs `fq`/`fq_codel` for pacing. BBRv2 adds a loss response above 2% (`beta = 0.3`, `loss_thresh = 0.02`), ECN response at 50%, and `inflight_hi` bounding; BBRv3 tightens queue bounds and mixed-fairness.

**Pacing** is not optional: releasing a 10 MB window as one ACK-clocked burst takes 400 ms to drain at line rate — the buffer must absorb the entire burst. Pacing at BtlBw spreads it over the RTT.

**AQM** caps the standing queue independently of the sender. CoDel targets a 5 ms sojourn with a 100 ms interval — but 100 ms < 400 ms RTT, so on this path the control loop over-reacts; FQ-CoDel (per-flow queues, sparse-flow priority) is the safer choice, CAKE adds per-host fairness. At 200 Mbit/s, 5 ms = 125 kB.

**ECN + L4S/DCTCP** is the cleanest answer for delay: DCTCP marks at K = 65 packets (~0.38 ms here) and keeps the queue sub-millisecond; L4S targets a 1 ms queue (25 kB at this rate) with scalable CC (Prague), so the path runs at 401 ms instead of 800 ms. Requires AQM support end-to-end, which is why BBR is the more deployable fix.

**Loss recovery**: SACK + RACK/TLP (RFC 8985) eliminate most RTOs and repair multi-loss windows in 1–2 RTTs instead of k RTTs. On a 400 ms path each avoided RTO saves 3.8 s of slow start.

## 8. Summary

| Mechanism | Effect on 400 ms / 200 Mbit/s |
|---|---|
| Window scaling off | Hard cap 1.31 Mbit/s |
| Slow start (IW10) | 3.8 s to fill; ~90% idle during ramp |
| Reno AI | 29.2 kbit/s per RTT (0.0146% of capacity) |
| Reno at p=10⁻⁵ | 11.3 Mbit/s (5.6%); needs p ≤ 3.2×10⁻⁸ for full rate |
| Deep buffer (10 MB) | Permanent +400 ms, RTT 800 ms, 400 ms delay sawtooth |
| CUBIC | Recovery 17.3 s vs 1,370 s; still loss-driven, still bloats |
| BBR | ~200 Mbit/s at p=10⁻³; holds ~1.25–1.5× BDP queue |
| L4S/DCTCP | Sub-1 ms queue (25 kB) at 200 Mbit/s |
| RTO on this path | ~440 ms → 1 MSS → 3.8 s to recover |

The failure is a scaling mismatch: loss-based AIMD's control authority per RTT is 0.0146% of the link, while the path's feedback delay is 800 ms. CUBIC fixes the growth law; BBR fixes the *signal* — which is the change that actually matters, because on a 400 ms path random loss carries no information about congestion.
